The 106th Anti-Aircraft Brigade (106th AA Bde) was an air defence formation of the British Army during the Second World War. Formed in May 1943 from the re-organised and renamed 53rd AA Bde, it was initially attached to the First Canadian Army, but would go on to be one of two mobile anti-aircraft brigades allocated to the British Second Army for the campaign in North-West Europe, the other being the 100th AA Bde. In common with other anti-aircraft brigades, the unit took on anti-tank, river, ground and bridge defence.
The brigade landed in Normandy between 10 and 27 June 1944 and initially took on an air defence role at airfields in the beachhead, before covering river crossings and forward airfields in the breakout from Normandy. It formed part of the initial ground and air defences of Antwerp in September 1944, before going on to deploy in Operation Market Garden in defence of key bridges on XXX Corps' line of advance along "Hell's Highway".
In January 1945, the brigade considered its position to be unique in that it had guns deployed in four countries simultaneously, namely France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, and believed it was the first anti-aircraft brigade established on German soil. At the cessation of hostilities, the brigade was advanced enough to be within the Soviet occupation zone and withdrew to take on occupational duties in the British occupation zone, around Hamburg and Munsterlager. The brigade disbanded in April 1946.
Formation
The 106th AA Bde was formed in May 1943, after the reorganisation and renaming of 53rd AA Bde. That brigade had been formed at the 53rd Light Anti-Aircraft Brigade in 1939 as part of 4th Anti-Aircraft Division, based in North West England. It was commanded by Brigadier Cyril Ian Victor Jones, who commissioned into the Royal Artillery in December 1919. Following the reorganisation, the brigade rebased in the Bromley area of South East London.
The brigade’s initial strength consisted of the 108th Heavy Anti-Aircraft Regiment (108th HAA Rgt), 109th HAA Rgt, 165th HAA Rgt,109th Light Anti-Aircraft Regiment (109th LAA Rgt) and 4th Light Anti-Aircraft/Searchlight Battery (4th LAA/SL Bty), but it soon added to its strength 71st LAA Rgt. It was affiliated to First Canadian Army at the end of May 1943 for training purposes,  and the British brigade was given special dispensation to wear the Canadian army’s shoulder flash, omitting the “Canada” text above the badge.
The remainder of 1943 and beginning of 1944 saw the brigade alternating between active-duty air defence operations, mostly in defence of towns and airfields in South East England, and training exercises. “Exercise Salmon” in February and March 1944 consisted of a series of three three-week exercises working with the Royal Air Force, including “setting up in detail a well defended airfield as it would be overseas”. This contrasts with the training exercises that 100th AA Bde took part in, exercises “Lobster” and “Shrimp”, which focused on mobile operations.
Operation Overlord
The brigade began its landing in Normandy on D+4, 10 June 1944, and started airfield defence tasks within the beachhead under No. 83 Expeditionary Air Group, Second Tactical Air Force by 14 June. Twelve airfields had been planned, but the shallow beachhead meant that only eight were initially active. To its own strength of three HAA regiments and two LAA regiments, the brigade took under command ten light anti-aircraft squadrons of the RAF Regiment (see order of battle), though the brigade's own HAA regiments were redeployed to reinforce the artillery of VIII and XXX Corps on 23 June.
The brigade remained in defence of the airfields through July and into August, expanding its coverage as more airfields opened. It claimed seven enemy aircraft destroyed and five “probably destroyed” in June, sustaining nine casualties in the process, and its war diary describes a "very successful day for the Bde guns" on 14 July 1944, when 14 enemy aircraft were confirmed destroyed.
This was followed, though, by orders on 16 July that heavily restricted anti-aircraft guns situated more than 5000 yards behind the front line from engaging enemy aircraft, virtually restricting engagements to identified hostile aircraft committing a hostile act. The slower than planned expansion of the Normandy beachhead and density of guns meant that large areas of airspace, covered by anti-aircraft guns in IAZs|group="Note"}} and GDAs|group="Note"}}, were restricted to allied aircraft and handicapped air support for the front line. Contemporary orders also indicate that the measures were in part to protect allied aircraft from potential friendly fire incidents from “a few ill trained or indisciplined units or detachments”.
None of the areas that 106th AA Bde was responsible for were situated within 5000 yards of the front line, and as such “the restrictions vitally affected [the] brigade”. Routledge writes that the “deployment was frustrating for 106th AA Brigade as, not only were there surplus guns, but RAF airfield commanders refused all permission to engage unless the places were actually being attacked”. The orders were tightened and loosened at various stages over the following weeks, before the brigade ceased to be responsible for anti-aircraft defence of RAF airfields on 21 August and reverted to the command of Second Army.
Following the closing of the Falaise Pocket on 21 August, the brigade took on short-lived deployments in defence of the pontoon bridge crossings over the Seine and Somme rivers, just behind the front line of the advance of Second Army.
Advance into the Low Countries
Antwerp
On 3 September the brigade handed over its bridge defence commitments to 76th AA Bde and came under the command of XII Corps for the advance into Belgium. The brigade crossed the border on 5 September, initially deploying 113th LAA Rgt in defence of Ghent. On 8 September, the brigade began moving into Antwerp to take over defence of the city and port from 100th AA Bde, initially with 107th HAA Rgt, 108th HAA Rgt and 157 AAOR.
Though allied forces had entered Antwerp, German forces remained in the city and initially the guns of 107th HAA Rgt and 108th HAA Rgt deployed in a primarily ground role around the south of the city, acting as artillery support. Fire support was given to 53rd (Welsh) Infantry Division and 2nd Canadian Division, with shoots carried out against German withdrawal routes across the River Scheldt and strongpoints within Fort de Merksem. Once the west bank of the Scheldt came under allied control, 106th AA Bde took over defence of Antwerp port and 107th HAA Rgt reverted to an air-defence role.
Over the following days, the brigade expanded both its size and its duties further, with 71st LAA Rgt joining the brigade on 13 September and deploying for anti-aircraft defence for bridges over the Albert Canal at Geel and the Escaut Canal. On 24 September, the brigade was relieved in Antwerp and deployed deployed with Second Army to the Netherlands as part of Operation Market Garden.
Operation Market Garden
Winter in the Netherlands
On 8 November, the brigade was involved in a friendly fire incident with USAAF aircraft. Twelve P-47 Thunderbolt aircraft bearing USAAF markings mistakenly attacked the bridge across the River Meuse at Berg with bombs and cannon fire, injuring two people and damaging water and electricity mains. After a short delay, "which was understandable given the circumstances", light anti-aircraft guns opened fire and damaged four or five aircraft, all of which made it back to base.
On 13 November, Dutch civilians approached brigade HQ with reports that German soliders were hiding in a barge nearby. A search party was despatched, and three German soldiers were discovered as reported. Unteroffizier Heinz Fliegen, Obergefreiter Fritz Balgar and Obergefreiter Fritz Schwantaer had escaped from a POW camp in Arras nearly two weeks prior.
On 3 December, a conference held by Commander, Corps Royal Artillery of XXX Corps gave responsibility for the co-ordination of all anti-aircraft protection in the XXX Corps area to Brigadier Jones. 27th LAA Rgt, 94th LAA Rgt, 108th LAA Rgt and 110th LAA rgt were added to the brigade's strength to assist with the duty.
